statement: In healthy Japanese men aged 20 to 50 with the fully active form of the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, drinking water in between drinks while drinking sake, compared with the same sake without the extra water in another session, did not detectably change breath alcohol or acetaldehyde, or any of six symptom ratings the next morning (headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, flushing and feeling exhilarated), in a randomized crossover trial of 13 men; scores on a short speed-of-processing test were lower with water right after drinking, when several men felt bloated, and slightly but not significantly higher the next morning (Imai et al., 2026). Evidence is insufficient to say whether water during drinking changes hangover: the trial was small and open-label, reported no effect sizes or intervals, used no hangover scale, could detect only a very large effect, and was funded by the brewer of the sake used; because the amount of alcohol was fixed, it could not test whether water helps in real life by leading people to drink less or more slowly. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial with 13 men, drinking water between drinks did not change how much alcohol was in their breath or how they felt the next morning, compared with drinking the same alcohol without the water. The trial was too small to rule out a modest benefit, and it could not test whether water helps by making people drink less.
population: 13 healthy Japanese men aged 20 to 50 with the fully active ALDH2 genotype, studied in one clinical trial unit
exposure: Water drunk in between drinks during a supervised session of drinking sake (study amounts are on the study card)
comparator: The same men drinking the same sake without the added water in another session
outcome: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde; next-morning symptom ratings (headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, facial flushing, feeling exhilarated); Digit Symbol Substitution Test
magnitude: No numerical estimates or intervals reported. Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde: no significant difference at any time. Six symptom ratings: no significant difference at any time. Digit Symbol Substitution Test, change from the pre-drinking score: lower with water right after drinking (p = 0.01) and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08, called not significant by the authors). The authors put power at barely 0.8 for an effect size of 1 (one-sided).

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Discussions, 2nd paragraph (last sentence)
evidence.extracted: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde did not differ significantly between the water and no-water sessions at any time after drinking; acetaldehyde point estimates were slightly higher with water shortly after drinking, and the curves were almost identical by the next morning.

None of the six visual analogue ratings (facial flushing, headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, feeling exhilarated) differed significantly between the sessions at any time point; values are shown only in figures.

Digit Symbol Substitution Test change from baseline was lower with water right after drinking (p = 0.01), which the authors link to abdominal bloating from the large amount of fluid, and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08), described as not statistically significant.

The authors state that with 13 participants power was barely 0.8 for an effect size of 1, that all were men of one genotype, that the open-label design may have biased the ratings, and that the design cannot separate water between drinks from drinking the alcohol diluted.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions
evidence.locator: Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions
evidence.extracted: Funded by the sake brewer that made the test drink; four of eight authors were employed by its research laboratory, two of whom did the formal analysis, although the funding statement says the funder had no role in analysis.

risk_of_bias.note: Open label with self-rated symptoms, per-protocol analysis after one exclusion tied to the water condition, randomization not described, and no numerical results; card overall high risk, although the expected bias would favour water rather than the null.

indirectness.note: Men only, one genotype, one drink, one fixed amount of alcohol and a very large amount of water; the real-life question (does water help when people drink as they choose) was not tested.

imprecision.note: 13 participants, no intervals, power only for a very large effect.

grade.reasoning: A randomized crossover trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and twice for imprecision, giving very low. The relation is insufficient evidence rather than no detectable change, because no interval excludes a meaningful benefit (METHODS 6.3). Single study. The authors' suggestion that water may help in daily life by limiting how much people drink is not a finding of this trial.
